Richard Byfield
rich'ard bi'feeld
n. (Richard Byfield, c. 1598–1664, Westminster divine and defender of the sabbath)
Germanic Ricohard, strong in rule; English Byfield, dweller by the field.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Richard Byfield was rector of Long Ditton in Surrey, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and the author of a long vindication of the Lord's Day against those who held the fourth commandment wholly ceremonial and the Christian Sunday a matter of church custom only. He was ejected in 1662. His case was the ordinary Puritan one: that the commandment to keep one day in seven holy belongs to the moral law and binds all men, that the particular day was changed by apostolic authority to the first of the week in honour of the resurrection, and that the day is for worship, rest and mercy rather than for sport or trade. The dictionary holds that position. It also notes what the sabbath is for, since the word has acquired in modern use a reputation for severity which the fourth commandment does not have: the day is a gift of rest to a working people, and it is the only commandment that explicitly protects the servant and the stranger.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sabbath as a day of rest set apart for religious duties, and moral law as the law of God prescribing moral duties.

expand to see more

SAB'BATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest; among Christians, the first day of the week, in commemoration of our Saviour's resurrection.

MOR'AL, a. Relating to the practice, manners or conduct of men as social beings; as the moral law.

CEREMO'NIAL, a. Relating to ceremony or external rite; ritual.

VINDICA'TION, n. The act of vindicating; defense; justification against denial or censure.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:8 — "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."

Isa 58:13 — "If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:"

Mar 2:27 — "And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath:"

Heb 4:9 — "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God."

Modern Corruption

He vindicated the Lord's Day as moral law, and the day itself as rest and mercy rather than severity.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse cuts both ways. In one direction the fourth commandment is dismissed as a ceremony abolished in Christ, with the result that a Christian people works and trades seven days and wonders why it is exhausted. In the other, sabbath keeping becomes a competition in abstentions, and the day that was given for rest and mercy is made a burden — which our Lord addressed directly in the Gospels.

The principle to recover is that the day is commanded, is holy, and is a gift. “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8). It is to be a pleasure and not a privation: “call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable” (Isa 58:13). Its direction is settled by Christ Himself: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath” (Mar 2:27). And it points beyond itself — “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shabbath (H7676), a sabbath, a rest; Greek sabbatismos (G4520), a keeping of sabbath, a rest.

Usage

"“Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8) — a vindication of the Lord's Day."

"“call the sabbath a delight” (Isa 58:13) — rest and mercy, not a competition in abstentions."

"“The sabbath was made for man” (Mar 2:27) — ejected from Long Ditton in 1662."
